questions.analysis: for 【线索】condition for sth = …的条件 线索就在本句内：a necessary condition __(1)__ many worthwhile things。condition 【选项】A) on ✗ 搭配不当 on 不与 condition 构成"…的条件"之义，on condition that 是"以…为条件（从句）"，结构和这 B) like ✗ 语义不通 like 意为"像"，condition like things 读不通，无此搭配。 C) for ✓ 固定搭配契合 condition for sth 正是"…的必要条件"，for 把 condition 与其服务对象 many worthwhile things 接上，语法语义双合。 D) from ✗ 搭配错误 from 表来源，与 condition 不搭，无 condition from 之说。 【验证】代入读：a necessary condition __(1)__ many worthwhile things → a necessary condition for many worthwhile things，"许多好事的必要条件"，与下文 child care, friendships 这些"好事"举例自然衔接。

faith 【线索】全文主题词 trust 是同义线索 本句 putting your __(2)__ in the wrong place often carries a high 是上句 Trust is a tricky business. 的延续，put faith in = trust（信任），空处要与 trust 同义，指"把信任 【选项】 A) faith ✓ 与 trust 同义契合 put your faith in sth = 信任、信赖，正承接 Trust is a tricky business.，"把信任放错地方"， B) concern ✗ 义偏"担忧" C) attention ✗ 义偏"注意力" attention 是"注意力"，pay attention 才搭，与 trust 无同义关系。 D) interest ✗ 义偏"兴趣/利益" 【验证】代入：putting your faith in the wrong place often carries a high ___，"把信任托付错人 代价高昂"，正好对应第1段"on the other hand"的反面，与全局辩证脉络自洽。

price 【线索】wrong place 提示负面后果 线索在本句逻辑：putting your __(2)__ in the wrong place often carries a high __(3)__。"放错地方"是负面前提，carries a high ___ 应是"付出高昂代价"，high price（高 【选项】A) benefit ✗ 褒贬相反 B) debt ✗ 范围过窄 debt 是具体的"债务"，carry a high debt 偏指金钱负债，无法概括信任错位带来的各种代价。 C) hope ✗ 逻辑不符 hope 是"希望"，与负面后果无关，且 carry a high hope 不成立。 D) price ✓ 搭配+逻辑双契合 carry/pay a high price 是"付出高昂代价"的固定说法，正承接"信任放错地方"的负面前提，褒贬 【验证】代入：putting your faith in the wrong place often carries a high price，"信任错人往往

Then 【线索】第1段陈述两面→第2段顺势发问 第1段讲信任有风险，第2段 __(4)__, why do we trust at all? 顺着"既然有风险"自然抛出疑 【选项】A) Therefore ✗ 因果过强 B) Then ✓ 话题承接契合 Then = "那么"，承上文"信任既有益又有险"顺势发问 why do we trust at all?，是引出新问题的 C) Instead ✗ 转折无依据 D) Again ✗ 无重复语境 【验证】代入：Then, why do we trust at all?——"那么，我们究竟为何还要信任呢？"承接第1段的

When 【线索】"信任时"伴随"分泌催产素" 线索在主从句的同步关系：__(5)__ people place their trust in an individual or an institution, their brains release oxytocin——人一旦信任，大脑就释放催产素，是"当… 【选项】A) Until ✗ 时间逻辑反 B) Unless ✗ 条件相反 C) Although ✗ 无转折关系 D) When ✓ 同步伴随契合 【验证】代入：When people place their trust ..., their brains release oxytocin——"当人们信

produces 【线索】激素"产生"快感并"引发"本能 线索在并列结构：a hormone that __(6)__ pleasurable feelings and triggers the herding instinct。与 triggers（引发）并列，空处也应是"产生/带来"快感这一正向制 【选项】A) selects ✗ 义偏"挑选" selects 是"选择"，激素"选择"快感讲不通。 B) produces ✓ 产生义契合 produces = "产生、带来"，激素 produces pleasurable feelings，与并列的 triggers 同向，准 C) applies ✗ 搭配不当 applies 是"应用、涂抹"，apply feelings 不成立。 D) maintains ✗ 义偏"维持" 【验证】代入：a hormone that produces pleasurable feelings and triggers the herding instinct——"一种产生愉悦感并触发群居本能的激素"，与上句 because it feels good

connect 【线索】herding instinct 指向"联结" 线索在本句：triggers the herding instinct that prompts humans to __(7)__ with one 【选项】A) consult ✗ 义偏"咨询" B) compete ✗ 色彩相反 compete = "竞争"，与"群居、合群"的合作色彩相反。 C) connect ✓ 凝聚义契合 connect = "联结、与…亲近"，connect with one another 正是群居本能驱使下"彼此联系抱 团"，色彩与 herding instinct 一致。 D) compare ✗ 义偏"比较" compare = "比较"，与群居合群无关，逻辑跑偏。 【验证】代入：prompts humans to connect with one another——"促使人类彼此联结"，紧扣

to 【线索】exposure to sth = 接触某物 线索在本句搭配：exposure __(8)__ this hormone puts us in a trusting。exposure to = 【选项】A) at ✗ 搭配错误 at 不与 exposure 搭配。 B) by ✗ 搭配错误 by 与 exposure 不构成"接触"义。 C) of ✗ 搭配错误 of 虽常接名词，但 exposure of 多指"…的曝光/揭露"，与此处"接触激素"义不符。 D) to ✓ 固定搭配契合 to 构成 exposure to this hormone"接触这种激素"，是 expose 系列的固定介词，语法语义 【验证】代入：exposure to this hormone puts us in a trusting ___——"接触这种激素使我们进

mood 【线索】下文实验证明是"心境"变化 线索跨到下句：those subjects were ready to lend significantly higher amounts of trusting mood（信任心境）最贴。 【选项】A) context ✗ 义偏"语境/环境" B) mood ✓ 心境义契合 mood = "心境、情绪状态"，a trusting mood"信任的心境"，正是催产素作用于人内心、令其 C) period ✗ 义偏"时期" D) circle ✗ 义偏"圈子" 【验证】代入：puts us in a trusting mood——"使我们进入信任的心境"，与紧随其后"更愿借钱给

counterparts 【线索】实验对照组——吸入别物的另一半 线索在对比句：those subjects were ready to lend significantly higher amounts of money to strangers than were their __(10)__ who inhaled something else。前组吸催 产素、后组 inhaled something else，二者是同一实验里地位对应的两组人，即"对照者/对 应者"。 【选项】 A) counterparts ✓ 对应者义契合 B) substitutes ✗ 义偏"替代者" C) colleagues ✗ 义偏"同事" colleagues = "同事"，受试者之间无同事关系，无中生有。 D) supporters ✗ 义偏"支持者" supporters = "支持者"，与实验对照组身份无关。 【验证】代入：than were their counterparts who inhaled something else——"比吸入别的东西

Lucky 【线索】"有识谎第六感"是好事 线索在本句内容：__(11)__ for us, we also have a sixth sense for dishonesty that may 【选项】A) Funny ✗ 色彩不符 B) Lucky ✓ 褒义契合 C) Odd ✗ 色彩不符 D) Ironic ✗ 无反讽逻辑 【验证】代入：Lucky for us, we also have a sixth sense for dishonesty——"幸运的是，我们还

protect 【线索】识谎能力的作用=保护 线索在本句逻辑与第11空呼应：we also have a sixth sense for dishonesty that may __(12)__ us，既然第11空已定"Lucky for us（幸运）"，这第六感对人的作用就是"protect 【选项】A) monitor ✗ 义偏"监控" B) protect ✓ 保护义契合 protect = "保护"，识谎第六感 protect us（保护我们免遭欺骗），与 Lucky for us 的"幸运"评 C) surprise ✗ 逻辑不符 surprise = "使惊讶"，第六感"使我们惊讶"与"幸运、自保"逻辑不接。 D) delight ✗ 程度/方向偏 【验证】代入：a sixth sense for dishonesty that may protect us——"一种或能保护我们的识谎

between 【线索】differentiate between A and B 线索在本句结构：differentiate __(13)__ a credible person and a dishonest one——"在 【选项】 A) between ✓ 固定搭配契合 differentiate between A and B = "区分A和B"，between 与后文 a credible person and a dishonest one 的两者结构精确匹配。 B) within ✗ 搭配/逻辑错 within 表"在…之内"，differentiate within 不成立，且"两者之间"非"之内"。 C) toward ✗ 搭配错误 toward 表方向"朝向"，不与 differentiate 搭配。 D) over ✗ 搭配错误 over 与 differentiate 无搭配关系。 【验证】代入：differentiate between a credible person and a dishonest one——"区分可信者

introduced 【线索】实验里把幼儿"引见"给测试者 线索在本句场景：Sixty toddlers were each __(14)__ to an adult tester holding a plastic container——把每个幼儿"引见/带到"一位成人测试者面前开始实验，introduce sb to sb 【选项】A) transferred ✗ 义偏"转移" B) added ✗ 义偏"添加" added = "添加"，add toddlers to a tester 不通。 C) introduced ✓ 引见义契合 introduced = "引见、介绍给"，be introduced to an adult tester"被引见给一位成人测试者"， D) entrusted ✗ 义偏"托付" entrusted = "委托、托付"，entrust sb to sb 含"把人交托照管"，过重且不符"见面做实验"场景。 【验证】代入：Sixty toddlers were each introduced to an adult tester——"60名幼儿各自被引

inside 【线索】下文"找到玩具/容器是空的"指向往里看 线索在后句结果：Half of them found a toy; the other half __(16)__ the container was empty——孩子要发现容器里"有玩具/是空的"，必须 look inside（往里看），故 选 inside。 【选项】A) out ✗ 方向相反 out = "向外"，look out 是"往外看/当心"，与"看容器内部"方向相反。 B) back ✗ 方向不符 back = "往回看"，与"看容器里"无关。 C) around ✗ 范围不符 D) inside ✓ 向内义契合 inside = "往里面（看）"，look inside 正对应下文"发现里面有玩具或是空的"，方向精确。 【验证】代入：Each subject was then invited to look inside——"接着每个孩子被邀请往里看"，

discovered 【线索】与前半 found a toy 平行 线索在并列对照：Half of them found a toy; the other half __(16)__ the container was empty——前半"发现一个玩具"，后半应对称地"发现容器是空的"，discover 与 found 同 【选项】 A) discovered ✓ 发现义契合 discovered = "发现"，与前半 found a toy 平行对称，"另一半发现容器是空的"，语义结构 B) proved ✗ 义偏"证明" C) insisted ✗ 义偏"坚持声称" insisted = "坚持认为"，孩子是亲眼所见的事实，无需"坚称"。 D) remembered ✗ 逻辑不符 【验证】代入：the other half discovered the container was empty——"另一半发现容器是空 的"，与前半"found a toy"完美对称，引出下句"realized the tester had fooled them"，

fooled 【线索】假装有物=骗了孩子 线索在情节与第13空呼应：测试者看进空容器却 exclaiming, "Wow!"，孩子却 realized the tester had __(17)__ them——这正是"耍弄、欺骗"了孩子，与全段"a dishonest one （骗子）"主题对应，fooled（愚弄）最贴。 【选项】A) betrayed ✗ 程度过重 B) wronged ✗ 义偏"冤枉" wronged = "冤枉、不公正对待"，测试者是"骗"不是"冤枉"孩子。 C) fooled ✓ 愚弄义契合 fooled = "愚弄、欺骗"，准确描述"假装空容器里有东西"这一把戏，呼应第3段 dishonesty D) mocked ✗ 义偏"嘲笑" mocked = "嘲笑、戏弄"，重在"取笑"，而测试者是"骗"非"笑"孩子。 【验证】代入：realized the tester had fooled them——"意识到测试者骗了他们"，与上文"对着空

willing 【线索】信任→愿意配合 线索在本句因果：the majority were __(18)__ to cooperate with the tester ..., demonstrating that they trusted his leadership——既然"信任其领导"，多数孩子就"愿 意"配合，willing（愿意的）顺理成章。 【选项】A) forced ✗ 逻辑相反 B) willing ✓ 愿意义契合 willing = "愿意的"，be willing to cooperate"愿意配合"，正由"信任其领导"导出，褒贬逻辑 C) hesitant ✗ 态度相反 hesitant = "犹豫的"，与"信任、主动配合"相悖。 D) entitled ✗ 义偏"有权的" entitled = "有资格的"，be entitled to 表"有权做"，与"愿不愿意配合"的态度无关。 【验证】代入：the majority were willing to cooperate with the tester——"大多数孩子愿意配 合测试者"，与紧随的 they trusted his leadership 构成"因信任故愿意"的连贯因果，全局

In contrast 【线索】多数配合 vs 仅5人参与=对比 线索在前后两句的反差：前句 the majority were __(18)__ to cooperate（未被骗组多数配 合），本句 only five of the 30 children paired with the "__(20)__" tester participated （被骗组仅5人参与），是鲜明对比，故用 In contrast。 【选项】 A) In contrast ✓ 对比义契合 B) As a result ✗ 因果不成立 C) On the whole ✗ 义偏"总体上" On the whole = "总的来说"，用于总结归纳，而此处是两组对比、非总结。 D) For instance ✗ 非举例关系 【验证】代入：In contrast, only five of the 30 children ... participated——"相比之下，被骗组30

unreliable 【线索】对应前文"骗孩子的不诚实者" 线索回指第3段：测试者 had __(17)__ them（骗了孩子），与 a credible person and a dishonest one 中的"dishonest one"对应。骗子=不可信赖，故引号里贴的标签是 unreliable（不可靠的）。 【选项】A) inflexible ✗ 义偏"死板" inflexible = "僵化、不灵活"，测试者的问题是"骗人"而非"死板"。 B) incapable ✗ 义偏"无能力" incapable = "无能的"，测试者不是"没能力"，而是"不诚实"。 C) unreliable ✓ 不可信义契合 unreliable = "不可靠、不可信的"，正概括"骗了孩子"的测试者，与第3段 dishonest one 同义 D) unsuitable ✗ 义偏"不合适" 【验证】代入：only five of the 30 children paired with the "unreliable" tester participated OVERVIEW · 通读建境 开篇即定调：Trust is a tricky business.——信任既是育儿、友谊等好事的必要条件，放错地 第1段辩证抛出信任的两面 On the one hand / On the other hand；第2段答"为何信任"，归 因于催产素 why do we trust at all? Well, because it feels good.；第3段用 we also have a sixth sense for dishonesty 转向反面；第4段以婴儿能否识破骗子的实验结果收束 demonstrating that they trusted his leadership。把握这条"正—反"主线，是判断第11、19 SENTENCE INSIGHTS · 句子精讲 5 On the other hand, putting your faith in the wrong place often carries a high price. A Canadian study found that children as young as 14 months can differentiate between a credible person and a dishonest one. The tester would ask, "What's in here?" before looking into the container, smiling, and exclaiming, "Wow!" Among the children who had not been tricked, the majority were willing to cooperate with the tester in learning a new skill, demonstrating that they trusted his leadership. In contrast, only five of the 30 children paired with the "unreliable" tester participated in a follow-up activity. 本句在成分划分上有多个训练价值点：1) 复杂主语的范围确定（"only five of the 30...

sections.title: 阅读理解
sections.directions: Read the following four texts. Answer the questions after each text by choosing A, B, C or D. Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (40 points)

blocks.content: Among the annoying challenges facing the middle class is one that will probably go unmentioned in the next presidential campaign: What happens when the robots come for their jobs? Don't dismiss that possibility entirely. About half of U.S. jobs are at high risk of being automated, according to a University of Oxford study, with the middle class disproportionately squeezed. Lower-income jobs like gardening or day care don't appeal to robots. But many middle-class occupations – trucking, financial advice, software engineering – have aroused their interest, or soon will. The rich own the robots, so they will be fine. This isn't to be alarmist. Optimists point out that technological upheaval has benefited workers in the past. The Industrial Revolution didn't go so well for Luddites whose jobs were displaced by mechanized looms, but it eventually raised living standards and created more jobs than it destroyed. Likewise, automation should eventually boost productivity, stimulate demand by driving down prices, and free workers from hard, boring work. But in the medium term, middle-class workers may need a lot of help adjusting. The first step, as Erik Brynjolfsson and Andrew McAfee argue in The Second Machine Age, should be rethinking education and job training. Curriculums – from grammar school to college – should evolve to focus less on memorizing facts and more on creativity and complex communication. Vocational schools should do a better job of fostering problem-solving skills and helping students work alongside robots. Online education can supplement the traditional kind. It could make extra training and instruction affordable. Professionals trying to acquire new skills will be able to do so without going into debt. The challenge of coping with automation underlines the need for the U.S. to revive its fading business dynamism: Starting new companies must be made easier. In previous eras of drastic technological change, entrepreneurs smoothed the transition by dreaming up ways to combine labor and machines. The best uses of 3D printers and virtual reality haven't been invented yet. The U.S. needs the new companies that will invent them. Finally, because automation threatens to widen the gap between capital income and labor income, taxes and the safety net will have to be rethought. Taxes on low-wage labor need to be cut, and wage subsidies such as the earned income tax credit should be expanded: This would boost incomes, encourage work, reward companies for job creation, and reduce inequality. Technology will improve society in ways big and small over the next few years, yet this will be little comfort to those who find their lives and careers upended by automation. Destroying the machines that are coming for our jobs would be nuts. But policies to help workers adapt will be indispensable.

A new survey by Harvard University finds more than two-thirds of young Americans disapprove of President Trump's use of Twitter. The implication is that Millennials prefer news from the White House to be filtered through other sources, not a president's social media platform. Most Americans rely on social media to check daily headlines. Yet as distrust has risen toward all media, people may be starting to beef up their media literacy skills. Such a trend is badly needed. During the 2016 presidential campaign, nearly a quarter of web content shared by Twitter users in the politically critical state of Michigan was fake news, according to the University of Oxford. And a survey conducted for BuzzFeed News found 44 percent of Facebook users rarely or never trust news from the media giant. Young people who are digital natives are indeed becoming more skillful at separating fact from fiction in cyberspace. A Knight Foundation focus-group survey of young people between ages 14 and 24 found they use "distributed trust" to verify stories. They cross-check sources and prefer news from different perspectives – especially those that are open about any bias. "Many young people assume a great deal of personal responsibility for educating themselves and actively seeking out opposing viewpoints," the survey concluded. Such active research can have another effect. A 2014 survey conducted in Australia, Britain, and the United States by the University of Wisconsin-Madison found that young people's reliance on social media led to greater political engagement. Social media allows users to experience news events more intimately and immediately while also permitting them to re-share news as a projection of their values and interests. This forces users to be more conscious of their role in passing along information. A survey by Barna research group found the top reason given by Americans for the fake news phenomenon is "reader error," more so than made-up stories or factual mistakes in reporting. About a third say the problem of fake news lies in "misinterpretation or exaggeration of actual news" via social media. In other words, the choice to share news on social media may be the heart of the issue. "This indicates there is a real personal responsibility in counteracting this problem," says Roxanne Stone, editor in chief at Barna Group. So when young people are critical of an over-tweeting president, they reveal a mental discipline in thinking skills – and in their choices on when to share on social media.

Any fair-minded assessment of the dangers of the deal between Britain's National Health Service (NHS) and DeepMind must start by acknowledging that both sides mean well. DeepMind is one of the leading artificial intelligence (AI) companies in the world. The potential of this work applied to healthcare is very great, but it could also lead to further concentration of power in the tech giants. It is against that background that the information commissioner, Elizabeth Denham, has issued her damning verdict against the Royal Free hospital trust under the NHS, which handed over to DeepMind the records of 1.6 million patients in 2015 on the basis of a vague agreement which took far too little account of the patients' rights and their expectations of privacy. DeepMind has almost apologized. The NHS trust has mended its ways. Further arrangements – and there may be many – between the NHS and DeepMind will be carefully scrutinised to ensure that all necessary permissions have been asked of patients and all unnecessary data has been cleaned. There are lessons about informed patient consent to learn. But privacy is not the only angle in this case and not even the most important. Ms Denham chose to concentrate the blame on the NHS trust, since under existing law it "controlled" the data and DeepMind merely "processed" it. But this distinction misses the point that it is processing and aggregation, not the mere possession of bits, that gives the data value. The great question is who should benefit from the analysis of all the data that our lives now generate. Privacy law builds on the concept of damage to an individual from identifiable knowledge about them. That misses the way the surveillance economy works. The data of an individual there gains its value only when it is compared with the data of countless millions more. The use of privacy law to curb the tech giants in this instance feels slightly maladapted. This practice does not address the real worry. It is not enough to say that the algorithms DeepMind develops will benefit patients and save lives. What matters is that they will belong to a private monopoly which developed them using public resources. If software promises to save lives on the scale that drugs now can, big data may be expected to behave as a big pharma has done. We are still at the beginning of this revolution and small choices now may turn out to have gigantic consequences later. A long struggle will be needed to avoid a future of digital feudalism. Ms Denham's report is a welcome start.

The U.S. Postal Service (USPS) continues to bleed red ink. It reported a net loss of $5.6 billion for fiscal 2016, the 10th straight year its expenses have exceeded revenue. Meanwhile, it has more than $120 billion in unfunded liabilities, mostly for employee health and retirement costs. There are many reasons this formerly stable federal institution finds itself at the brink of bankruptcy. Fundamentally, the USPS is in a historic squeeze between technological change that has permanently decreased demand for its bread-and-butter product, first-class mail, and a regulatory structure that denies management the flexibility to adjust its operations to the new reality. And interest groups ranging from postal unions to greeting-card makers exert self-interested pressure on the USPS's ultimate overseer – Congress – insisting that whatever else happens to the Postal Service, aspects of the status quo they depend on get protected. This is why repeated attempts at reform legislation have failed in recent years, leaving the Postal Service unable to pay its bills except by deferring vital modernization. Now comes word that everyone involved – Democrats, Republicans, the Postal Service, the unions and the system's heaviest users – has finally agreed on a plan to fix the system. Legislation is moving through the House that would save USPS an estimated $28.6 billion over five years, which could help pay for new vehicles, among other survival measures. Most of the money would come from a penny-per-letter permanent rate increase and from shifting postal retirees into Medicare. The latter step would largely offset the financial burden of annually pre-funding retiree health care, thus addressing a long-standing complaint by the USPS and its unions. If it clears the House, this measure would still have to get through the Senate – where someone is bound to point out that it amounts to the bare, bare minimum necessary to keep the Postal Service afloat, not comprehensive reform. There's no change to collective bargaining at the USPS, a major omission considering that personnel accounts for 80 percent of the agency's costs. Also missing is any discussion of eliminating Saturday letter delivery. That common-sense change enjoys wide public support and would save the USPS $2 billion per year. But postal special-interest groups seem to have killed it, at least in the House. The emerging consensus around the bill is a sign that legislators are getting frightened about a politically embarrassing short-term collapse at the USPS. It is not, however, a sign that they're getting serious about transforming the postal system for the 21st century.

options.B: making more investment in new vehicles.

questions.analysis: 【判型】can be addressed by 问的是“通过什么手段可以解决”，属于对原文中明确解决方案的 【拆句】The long-standing complaint by the USPS and its unions can be addressed by____ 是 【定位】P3 Most of the money would come from a penny-per-letter permanent rate increase and from shifting postal retirees into Medicare. blocks.content: estimates for a new State Department Building. The commission was also to consider possible arrangements for the War and Navy Departments. To the horror of some who expected a Greek Revival twin of the Treasury Building to be erected on the other side of the White House, the elaborate French Second Empire style design by Alfred Mullett was selected, and construction of a building to house all three departments began in June of 1871. story library (completed in 1876), Diplomatic Reception Room, and Secretary's office decorated with carved wood, Oriental rugs, and stenciled wall patterns. The Navy Department moved into the east wing in 1879, where elaborate wall and ceiling stenciling and marquetry floors decorated the office of the Secretary. Departments most intimately associated with formulating and conducting the nation's foreign policy in the last quarter of the nineteenth century and the first quarter of the twentieth century – the period when the United States emerged as an international power. The building has housed some of the nation's most significant diplomats and politicians and has been the scene of many historic events. within the EEOB's granite walls. Theodore and Franklin D. Roosevelt, William Howard Taft, Dwight D. Eisenhower, Lyndon B. Johnson, Gerald Ford, and George H. W. Bush all had offices in this building before becoming president. It has housed 16 Secretaries of the Navy, 21 Secretaries of War, and 24 Secretaries of State. Winston Churchill once walked its corridors and Japanese emissaries met here with Secretary of State Cordell Hull after the bombing of Pearl Harbor.

options.E: The Eisenhower Executive Office Building (EEOB) commands a unique position in both the national history and the architectural heritage of the United States. Designed by Supervising Architect of the Treasury, Alfred B. Mullett, it was built from 1871 to 1888 to house the growing staffs of the State, War, and Navy Departments, and is considered one of the best examples of French Second Empire architecture in the country.
options.F: Construction took 17 years as the building slowly rose wing by wing. When the EEOB was finished, it was the largest office building in Washington, with nearly 2 miles of black and white tiled corridors. Almost all of the interior detail is of cast iron or plaster; the use of wood was minimized to insure fire safety. Eight monumental curving staircases of granite with over 4,000 individually cast bronze balusters are capped by four skylight domes and two stained glass rotundas.
options.G: The history of the EEOB began long before its foundations were laid. The first executive offices were constructed between 1799 and 1820. A series of fires (including those set by the British in 1814) and overcrowded conditions led to the construction of the existing Treasury Building. In 1866, the construction of the North Wing of the Treasury Building necessitated the demolition of the State Department building.
